content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified that approximately 250 million children globally are at risk of not reaching their developmental potential within the first five years of life. This underscores the critical importance of policies and programs that empower caregivers to support the developmental needs of young children. Evidence published in the 2017 Lancet series on early childhood development emphasizes the significance of nurturing care, which includes caregiver practices related to health, nutrition, safety, security, responsive caregiving, and early learning opportunities. These elements collectively contribute to the healthy development of children. The health sector plays a pivotal role in delivering essential nurturing care interventions, particularly during the first three years of life, a period of rapid brain development. This sector has the unique ability to reach the youngest children and their caregivers, promoting protective care and mitigating risk factors during this sensitive developmental window. To strengthen this approach, WHO aims to develop evidence-based guidelines to improve early childhood development (ECD). These guidelines will assist Member States in making informed decisions about policies and programs that align with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) related to health, learning, and behavior. The guidelines will complement existing WHO tools and recommendations relevant to nurturing care. A Guideline Development Group (GDG), comprising experts in ECD and health, has proposed four key research questions to inform recommendations on early learning and responsive caregiving. These questions address the effectiveness of responsive caregiving, early learning promotion, caregiving for socioemotional and behavioral development, and combined caregiving and nutrition programs on ECD outcomes in the first three years of life. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the evidence for these questions, analyzing 67 studies across the four research areas. The outcomes assessed included ECD, child attachment, behavior, growth, health, nutrition, caregiving practices, caregiver-child interactions, and caregiver mental health. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. Final recommendations will be determined by the GDG, informed by evidence-to-decision frameworks. The systematic review also highlighted challenges in the literature, such as inconsistent definitions and operationalization of nurturing care components like responsive caregiving and early learning support. To address this, the review process established clear definitions for these components, which evolved iteratively during data extraction and analysis. While broad categorizations were feasible, the potential for overlap across intervention strategies was acknowledged. The WHO guidelines aim to consolidate effective ECD-specific interventions, identify feasible delivery approaches, and integrate these into health and other services. The target audience includes health managers, workers, development agencies, implementing partners, NGOs, and policymakers in maternal and child health. The guideline development process follows the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development, ensuring a rigorous and systematic approach. In summary, the WHO's efforts to develop evidence-based guidelines for ECD interventions reflect a commitment to improving developmental outcomes for children globally. By addressing key research questions and synthesizing evidence, these guidelines will provide a comprehensive framework for nurturing care, supporting the health, learning, and well-being of young children.
